result.summary: The river-gods gather at Tempe to console or congratulate Peneus, but Inachus stays hidden, weeping for his lost daughter Io. Jupiter had seen Io, urged her into the grove, and when she fled he covered the earth in darkness and raped her.

scenes.title: Rivers gather at Tempe
scenes.summary: The valley of Tempe and the cavern of the river Peneus are described. Neighbouring rivers come to him, unsure whether to congratulate or console.

scenes.title: Inachus mourns alone
scenes.summary: Inachus hides in his cavern, weeping and fearing the worst about his missing daughter Io.
scenes.stakes: He has lost his daughter and does not know whether she lives.

scenes.title: Jupiter pursues Io
scenes.summary: Jupiter urges Io into the shady grove, boasting of his power. She flees past Lerna, and he covers the land in darkness and seizes her.
scenes.stakes: Io's freedom and chastity are threatened by a god she cannot outrun.

alias_notes.explanation: Jove is another name for Jupiter, king of the gods.

notable_quotes.reason: Jupiter's boastful appeal to his own power as he chases the fleeing Io.

analysis.text: Divine desire overrides consent, a recurring pattern in the Metamorphoses. Io's suffering begins here and leads to her transformation.
Ovid links myth to real landscape, such as Tempe and the Thessalian rivers, giving the tales a sense of place and local tradition.

legacy.text: The story of Jupiter and Io inspired many later artworks, including Correggio's painting Jupiter and Io (c. 1530).

fun_facts.text: Tempe was a famous beautiful valley in Thessaly, and later writers used its name for any lovely, shady retreat.

language_notes.text: Hæmonia is an old name for Thessaly in northern Greece, where the valley of Tempe lies.
"Congratulate or console": the rivers are unsure whether Io's disappearance is an honour (a god's favour) or a loss for her father.
"Worthy of Jove" and "I know not whom" is a coy boast: Jupiter implies the lucky husband is himself.
"Forced her modesty" is a euphemism for rape.

context_notes.text: Peneus is the chief river of Thessaly, and Tempe is its famous wooded gorge between Mounts Olympus and Ossa.
Inachus is the river-god of Argos and father of Io; as a river he weeps and swells his own waters.
Jupiter (Greek Zeus) is king of the gods and wields the thunderbolt, which is why he cites lightning.

literary_notes.text: The father's uncertain grief, believing her nowhere because he cannot find her, makes his suffering moving, and his tears literally feed his stream.
Jupiter offers protection from wild beasts while he is himself the danger; his power is used as a threat.
Darkness spread over the land mirrors the violence and hides it, ending the chase abruptly.
